extracted.intended_audience: scientists, natural philosophers, and educated readers interested in methodology of physiology and astronomy
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and methodological criteria for assessing scientific hypotheses (illustrated via physiology/social analogy and the Nebular Hypothesis). Emphasizes combining deductive and inductive reasoning, empirical evidence, analogy, and critical appraisal of observational inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use and limits of the deductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductive method can elucidate extremely general questions in physiology but its conclusions imply limits: more special phenomena of organization cannot always be dealt with deductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deduction to clarify very general principles, but recognize that particular, specialized phenomena often require other approaches (e.g., empirical/inductive methods) because specific outcomes depend on many contingent factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on the empirical method (especially in paleontology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paleontology and similar sciences must depend on empirical observation rather than pure deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fossil species' historical modifications are contingent on a variety of circumstances (season, latitude, etc.); empirical evidence is essential because deductive necessity does not determine specific form changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize individual variability and avoid assuming necessary correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to the same disturbance vary between individuals; an alteration in one organ does not necessitate a particular set of changes in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming strict, uniform mechanical or functional correlations across individuals — examples include bricks stacked/falling, locomotive idiosyncrasies, different physiological reactions (vaccination, alcohol, opium, tobacco). Such variability limits mechanistic deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy (sociological method) cautiously as a supplement
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of physiological phenomena with social phenomena can provide useful insights and suggest hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical reasoning can reveal similar principles (division of labour, integrations/differentiations, organ-like institutions) and suggest new avenues of inquiry, but avoid crude one-to-one correspondences and acknowledge differences between domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the genealogical pedigree of ideas as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracing an idea's ancestry (its intellectual pedigree) offers a rough index of its plausibility: high derivation (from law, mathematics, or rigorous theory) is supportive; low origin (mythology/anthropomorphism) is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical/philosophical parentage (e.g., derivation from gravitation theory) alongside empirical data when judging a hypothesis' credibility, but treat pedigree as only prima facie, not decisive, evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine a priori theoretical grounding with a posteriori empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is strongest when it has both solid theoretical parentage (a priori reasons) and abundant, varied observational evidence (a posteriori reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather and present multiple kinds of evidence; theoretical plausibility (e.g., consistency with universal gravitation) plus a wide array of observations together yield high probability for a hypothesis (as argued for the Nebular Hypothesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain observed distributional patterns without invoking improbable coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory hypothesis must account for spatial/distributional facts (e.g., nebulae being found in star-sparse regions) rather than attributing them to luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many cases would require extreme coincidences under an alternative explanation (e.g., remote galaxies coinciding with local star-poor spots), prefer hypotheses that provide a natural causal account of those distributional regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer distance (or other physical quantities) solely from apparent brightness/visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent magnitude or resolvability is not a reliable proxy for distance; Herschel's assumption that apparent size correlates mainly with distance is gratuitous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct measures (parallax, other metrics) and be wary of inferring scale simply from how visible or resolvable an object appears; counterexamples (e.g., 61 Cygni) show faintness does not guarantee remoteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check consistency between observational capabilities and hypothesized scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses must be consistent with what instruments logically can and cannot resolve given assumed distances and scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether an instrument that resolves a putatively remote object into parts could, under the same assumptions, resolve nearer structures; contradictions (e.g., resolving external nebulae into stars while failing to resolve the Milky Way) indicate the hypothesis needs re-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of current observable process is not decisive against past occurrence; consider historical possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a process (e.g., nebular condensation) is not presently observable, it may have occurred in the past — lack of contemporary examples does not alone refute a historical hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the expectation of present observability carefully; ask whether theory and remaining evidence make historical occurrence plausible and whether the absence itself requires an explanation before rejecting the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically contest and examine recent conclusions and alternative interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly asserted refutations or reinterpretations (e.g., Lord Rosse's resolving nebulae into stars) must be critically examined for incongruities and unwarrantable inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept apparent disconfirmatory discoveries at face value; analyze underlying assumptions, distributional facts, and logical consequences, and consider whether alternative interpretations better fit the totality of evidence.
